summary: This unit teaches you to write short technical reports at work: incident and near-miss reports, inspection reports, progress reports, job completion reports and test records. You will learn to find out who the report is for, gather accurate facts at the time, keep facts apart from opinions, set the report out with clear headings, write in plain language with correct numbers and units, use tables, photos and sketches, fill in forms, check your work, and hand in and keep reports safely.

blocks.p: This unit is shared by several programmes, including Welding and Electrical Installation. Every tradesperson writes reports: a welder reports a cracked weld or a near miss in the bay; an electrician records test readings and tells a customer what was installed; both write progress reports, fill in incident forms and inspection checklists. A **technical report** passes on clear, accurate facts so that someone else can make a decision or take action.

You do not need to be a great writer. You need to collect the facts carefully, keep to them, set them out in a sensible order and use plain words. A short, accurate report is worth far more than a long one full of guesses.
**Who it is for:** Level 2 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and new workers in any trade who must write reports, fill in forms and keep records.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Find out why it is needed, who will read it, when it is due and what form or template to use.
Make notes, measurements, readings, photos and sketches at the time, and take witnesses' accounts in their own words.
Tell facts from opinions, write exactly what was found, and be honest, including about your own mistakes.
Use a title, an introduction, findings, a conclusion and numbered recommendations, with headings.
Use plain words and short sentences, explain trade terms and abbreviations, and give every measurement its unit.
Show many items or readings in a table, and add captioned photos and labelled sketches.
Incident and near-miss reports, inspection reports, progress reports, job completion reports and test records.
Complete every box, use N/A, and correct mistakes the accepted way, on paper or on a phone or computer.
Check, hand in and keep reports
Check facts, figures and spelling, have the report checked, sign and date it, hand it to the right person, and file it securely.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the purpose of reports, types of report, gathering facts, facts and opinions, structure, language, numbers and units, tables and photos, forms, incident reports, checking, and handing in and filing.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as appendix, summary, e.g., approx., PDF and time sheet, and simple sums with dates, times and units) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: a group safety inspection of a workshop area with an inspection report, and the investigation of a staged near miss with an incident form and a short incident report. The assessor watches how you gather facts, how you work as a team, and how clearly you write and report.

blocks.note: In essay answers, write in full sentences and give reasons. "I write the report while the facts are fresh, so that the times and measurements are right" earns more than "write it quickly".
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A report is written for a **reader** who needs the facts to do something: fix a fault, pay a bill, stop an accident happening again, or accept a finished job. Before you write, ask: **who will read this, and what do they need from it?**

head: Reader
What they need
rows: What you found or did, the problems, what should happen next, and any cost or delay
What was done, in everyday words; anything that changed; how to look after the work; the warranty
Evidence of the work you did and how you did it
A safety officer, inspector or insurer
Exact facts: dates, times, places, people, causes and what has been done
Technical details: sizes, readings, settings and the state of the equipment

blocks.p: Choose the words and the amount of detail to suit the reader. A supervisor wants the readings; a customer wants to know the gate is finished and how to care for it.

head: Report
When it is written
What it contains
rows: After someone is hurt, or property or equipment is damaged
What happened, in order; the injury and first aid; witnesses; causes; actions to stop it happening again
After an event that could have hurt someone or caused damage, but did not
What happened and why; how to stop it happening again
After checking an area, a machine or a set of equipment against a checklist
What was checked; what was found; what must be done
When equipment or work is found to be faulty
The item, the fault, how it was found, what has been done to make it safe
Part-way through a job, often weekly
What is done, what is left, problems and delays, what happens next
When a job is finished, often for the customer
The work done, materials, changes, tests, care advice, warranty, customer's signature
When tests are carried out, such as electrical installation tests or weld tests
What was tested, the instrument, each reading with its unit, the date and the tester
When a machine or tool is serviced or repaired
Date, item and number, work done, parts used, who did it
Hours spent on each job, the work done and the materials used

blocks.note: A danger that could hurt someone soon (a live cable, a gas leak, a blocked fire exit) is reported **by word of mouth straight away**. The written report follows; it never replaces the warning.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Find out **why** the report is needed and **who** asked for it.
Find out **who will read it** and **when it is due**.
Find out whether there is a **form or template** to use: many workplaces have their own.
Collect what you need: a notebook or the form, a pen, a tape measure, the right test instrument, and a phone or camera if photos are allowed.

blocks.h: Record the facts at the time

blocks.p: Memory fades fast and mixes up details. Make **notes, measurements and photos at the time**, while you are looking at the thing you are reporting on, not at the end of the week.

ul: Write the date, the time and the exact place at the top of your notes.
Write down what you see, measure and read, with units, and the instrument you used.
Note serial numbers, asset numbers, circuit numbers and job numbers.
Take photos and make a quick sketch with the main sizes.
Write down the names of the people involved and of any witnesses.

blocks.h: Who, what, when, where, why and how

head: Question
Example of what to find out
rows: Who was involved, who saw it, who was told, who did the work
What happened or what was found; what equipment and materials; what injury or damage
The date and the exact time; how long it lasted
The exact place: "Welding Bay 3, beside the cutting bench", not "in the shop"
The causes, as far as the facts show them
How it happened, step by step; how it was found; how it was made safe

ul: Use the right instrument and check that it works before you rely on it.
Write the reading exactly as the instrument shows it, **with the unit**, for example 2.5 mm, 112 V or more than 200 MΩ.
Say what was measured and where: "Gap between the gate and the post at the top hinge: 12 mm."
Do not round readings off or change them to look better.
Talk to each witness **on their own**, as soon as possible, before they talk it over with others.
Ask **open questions** that let them tell it their way, such as "Tell me what you saw."
Do not put words in their mouth with **leading questions**, such as "He was running, wasn't he?"
Write down what they say **in their own words**, without changing or tidying it. Read it back to them and ask them to sign it if the form asks for that.
Record only what they saw and heard themselves, not what someone else told them.

head: Kind of question
Example
Use
rows: Gets the full account; use these most
Checks one fact; use them to fill gaps
"You forgot to chain it, didn't you?"
Suggests the answer; do not use them

flow: Make the area safe and give first aid first
If it is safe to leave things as they are, photograph and measure the scene before anything is moved
Make a labelled sketch showing where people and things were

blocks.note: Never put yourself or anyone else at risk to keep a scene as it was. If something must be moved to make the area safe, move it, and write down what was moved and why.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **fact** is something that can be seen, measured or checked, and it is the same whoever writes it down. An **opinion** is what a person thinks or feels, and someone else may think differently. Reports are used to make decisions about safety, repairs and money, so they must be built on facts.

head: Opinion or vague statement
Fact the reader can use
rows: "3 of the 12 fillet welds on the frame have undercut about 1 mm deep along the top toe."
"The cable to the kitchen outlet has no outer sheath for 150 mm behind the fridge, and the inner insulation is cracked."
"The welding machine's overheat lamp came on after 4 minutes of welding at 160 A."
"He was not wearing gloves when he picked up the plate."
"The root gap measured 4 mm; the drawing gives 2 mm."

blocks.h: Words to avoid, and what to write instead

ul: **Big, small, wide, a lot, some, a few:** give the number and the unit.
**Soon, a while ago, recently:** give the date and the time.
**Old, bad, poor, dodgy, damaged:** say exactly what is wrong and where.
**I think, I feel, probably:** leave them out unless you are giving a marked opinion.

blocks.p: Sometimes the reader wants your judgement, for example whether a machine is fit to use. Then mark it clearly as an opinion and give the facts it rests on: "In my opinion the holder should not be used, because its insulation is cracked for 20 mm and the jaws are loose."

ul: Report what really happened, even if it shows a mistake, including your own. A hidden mistake cannot be put right.
Never change dates, times or readings, and never leave out a fact because the reader may not like it.
A report may be used later as **evidence**: in a complaint, an insurance claim or an accident inquiry. A false report can harm people and cost you your job.
Write about **causes, not blame**. "The cylinder was not chained" helps to stop it happening again; "Oshane is careless" does not.

blocks.note: Blaming someone does not fix anything. A report that says what happened and why lets the workplace remove the cause, so the next person is safe.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Most short reports follow the same order. Headings and numbered sections help the reader find each part quickly.

head: Part
What goes in it
rows: What the report is about, in a few words: "Inspection of Welding Bay 2"
The date, the writer's name, who it is for, and any job or reference number
The main findings and the most urgent actions in a few lines, at the start, for a busy reader
Why the report was written, what it covers, and when and how the work was done
The facts: what was seen, measured, tested or done, in a sensible order, with tables, photos and sketches
What the findings mean, summed up. It brings in no new facts
What should be done next, by whom and by when; numbered, most urgent first
Extra material at the end: the full checklist, test sheets, witness statements, price lists
The writer's name, signature and the date

blocks.note: Plan the headings before you write, and sort your notes under them. Then the report almost writes itself.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Inspection of Welding Bay 2.** Date: Monday 9 November 2026. Written by: Kevin Morgan, Level 2 trainee. For: Mr Delroy Shaw, Workshop Supervisor.

**1 Introduction.** On 9 November 2026, from 09:00 to 09:30, I inspected Welding Bay 2 with the Centre's welding bay checklist, to check that it was safe before Wednesday's practical. I looked only; I did not open, switch on or adjust anything.
**2 Findings.**

head: Item
Finding
Photo
rows: On its bracket; seal and pin in place; service label dated 03/2026
Torn at the bottom for about 300 mm
Insulation on the handle cracked for about 20 mm

blocks.p: **3 Conclusion.** The bay is mostly in good order, but the electrode holder on machine 2 is not safe to use, and the torn screen does not fully protect people outside the bay.

**4 Recommendations.** 4.1 Take the electrode holder on machine 2 out of use today and replace it (Workshop Supervisor). 4.2 Repair or replace the torn screen before Wednesday's practical (Maintenance).
Signed: K. Morgan. Date: 09/11/2026. Appendix: completed checklist.

blocks.note: The cracked holder is a danger, so the trainee would also have told the supervisor **at once**, by word of mouth, before writing this report.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Use **short sentences**, with one idea in each.
Use **everyday words**: "use" rather than "utilise", "about" rather than "in the region of".
Say who did what: "I switched off the machine" is clearer than "The machine was switched off".
Use the past tense for what happened, and keep to it.
Use **exact** words: "the top hinge is cracked", not "there is a problem with the gate".
Explain a trade term the reader may not know, and write an **abbreviation in full the first time**: "residual current device (RCD)", then RCD.
No slang, text-speak or emojis, even in a message on a phone.
Keep it as **short as it can be while still giving all the facts**.

head: Unclear
Plain
rows: "It has been observed that the gate hinge appears to be in a state of failure."
"The top hinge on the gate is cracked."
"Attention is required to the electrical item at some point."
"Replace the cracked socket outlet in the kitchen this week."
"The outer sheath of the lead is split for 40 mm."
"Work was done on the machine by somebody."
"Mr Shaw replaced the fuse in the machine's plug at 10:15."

head: Short form
Meaning
Example
rows: PPE, e.g. gloves and safety glasses
That is (it explains exactly what you mean)
The main switch, i.e. the switch by the door
Used in a form box that does not apply

ul: **Every measurement has its unit.** "The gap was 3" could mean 3 mm or 3 m.
Leave a space between the number and the symbol: 25 mm, 220 V, 34 °C.
Unit symbols never take an s and are not followed by a full stop: write 25 mm, never 25 mms or 25 m.m.
Small and capital letters matter: mm (millimetre) is not MM; kW, not KW; m means metre but M means mega (a million).
Write 0.5, not .5, so the decimal point is not missed.
In Jamaica, dates written in numbers are **day/month/year**: 05/03/2026 is 5 March 2026.
American readers read numbers the other way round (month/day/year). When a report may be read abroad, or the date matters, **write the month in words**: 5 March 2026.
The **24-hour clock** avoids mixing up morning and afternoon: 14:30 is 2:30 p.m.; 09:15 is 9:15 a.m.
Give exact times where you can: "at about 14:15", not "after lunch".

head: Sum
Example
rows: Should be 100 mm, measures 98 mm: 100 − 98 = 2 mm undersize

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, and check that the answer makes sense. A 6 m bar cannot weigh 2 tonnes, and a job cannot take 900 hours a week.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A picture or a table can show in seconds what would take a page of words. Use them where they help the reader, number them, and refer to each one in the text ("see Photo 2", "Table 1").

head: Tool
Use it when
How to do it well
rows: There are many items or readings: ten extinguishers, a set of test results, a list of faults
Clear column headings, with units in the headings
Number it (Table 1) and give it a title
The reader needs to see exactly what was found: a crack, a burnt cable, a blocked exit
Clear, in focus, close enough to show the detail
An overall shot and a close-up
A rule or tape in the picture to show the size
A caption saying what, where and when
A position, a route or a shape matters: where a ladder stood, where a pipe runs, the shape of a broken bracket
Neat and labelled, with the main sizes
Marked NTS (not to scale) if it is not to scale
Landmarks such as doors, benches and walls

blocks.p: Every photo needs a **caption** that tells the reader what it shows, where and when: "Photo 2: cracked insulation on the electrode holder handle, machine 2, Welding Bay 2, 09/11/2026, 09:20." A photo with no caption leaves the reader guessing.

ul: Ask permission before you photograph people, and photograph equipment and places rather than faces where you can.
Do not include customers' private details (an address on a letter, a car's number plate) unless the report needs them.
Never edit a photo to change what it shows.
Use a work phone or camera where the workplace says so, and move the photos into the work folder.

sections.title: Incident, inspection, progress and completion reports

blocks.p: Write an **incident report** after anyone is hurt, or equipment or property is damaged, and a **near-miss report** after something happens that could have caused harm but did not. A near miss is a free warning: the same cause may hurt someone next time.

ul: Write it **as soon as possible**, the same day, while the facts are fresh. Tell the supervisor at once.

Give: the date, time and exact place; the names of the people involved and of witnesses; what the person was doing, with what equipment and PPE; what happened, **in the order it happened**; the injury and the first aid given, and by whom; what was done straight away to make the area safe; the causes; and recommendations.
Keep to facts, not blame.
Sign it, date it and hand it to the supervisor; make sure it is entered in the accident book or on the workplace's form.

head: Part
Example (a burn in the welding bay)
rows: Trainee Shanoya Brown, Tuesday 3 November 2026, about 10:20, Welding Bay 1
Moving a 6 mm plate she had just welded, wearing a leather apron and safety glasses but no gloves
She picked up the plate by its welded end, which was still hot, and dropped it
A burn about 30 mm across on the palm of her right hand; the first-aider, Mr Shaw, cooled it under running water for 20 minutes and covered it with cling film
Plate marked HOT and moved to the cooling rack with tongs
Gloves not worn; hot work not marked
1. Remind all trainees to wear gauntlets when handling welded work (Instructor, at the next class). 2. Mark all hot work with soapstone and use tongs (all trainees, from today).

flow: Agree the area with the supervisor and get the checklist
Wear the PPE the area needs
Walk through and check each item by looking only: do not open, switch on or repair anything
Record each finding at the time, with the place and condition, and take photos
Report any serious danger to the supervisor straight away
Write the report: introduction, findings table, conclusion, recommendations
Sign, date and hand it in

ul: What has been done since the last report, with numbers ("4 of the 6 classrooms wired").
What is left to do.
Problems and delays, with the reasons ("ceiling boards delivered 5 days late").
What happens next and when the job is expected to finish.
Anything the reader must do or decide, such as approving extra materials.

blocks.p: A **job completion report** tells the customer (and your own office) what was done. It should include:

ul: The business's name, the customer's name and address, the job number and the date the work was finished.

The work done, in plain words: "Fitted one pair of steel driveway gates, 3.6 m wide overall, with a drop bolt and a padlock bracket" or "Installed four outdoor LED security lights with a light sensor".
The main materials used.
Anything that is **different from the quotation**, with the reason and any change in price.
Tests carried out (for electrical work, with the test record attached or referred to).
Problems found, such as a weak wall or an old cable, and advice on them.
Care advice, such as touching up paint or keeping sensors clean, and the warranty.
Space for the customer to sign that the work is complete.
Identify exactly what was tested: the circuit number, the machine or the weld number.
Name the test and the instrument (with its number, if it has one).
Write each reading with its unit, exactly as shown.
Note whether each result meets the required value that the standard, the specification or the supervisor gives.
Date and sign it.

sections.title: Forms, checking, handing in and keeping records

blocks.p: Many workplaces use printed forms or forms on a phone or tablet. Everyone records the same information in the same way, so nothing is forgotten and reports can be compared.

ul: Read the whole form before you start.
Use a pen (black or blue), and write in **block capitals** where the form asks.
Fill in **every box**. Where a box does not apply, write **N/A** (not applicable), so the reader knows you did not just miss it.
Never make up an answer to fill a box.
Sign and date the form.

blocks.p: **Strike through** the mistake with one line so it can still be read, write the correct entry beside it, and **initial** it (and date it if the form asks). Do not use correction fluid, scribble over the mistake or tear part of the form off: the reader must be able to see what was changed and who changed it.

blocks.h: Reports on a phone or computer

ul: Use the workplace's template if there is one.
Give the file a clear name, for example the date, the job number and the type of report: 2026-11-09_Job1142_inspection.
Save it in the **agreed work folder**, not on the desktop or your own phone, and make sure it is **backed up** to a second place.
Send finished reports as a **PDF**, which looks the same on every device and is hard to change.
Protect files with a password where the workplace says so. Never post reports or work photos on personal social media or in group chats.

head: Check
Ask yourself
rows: Does it answer what I was asked? Does it have all its parts?
Does every fact, measurement and reading match my notes? Does every number have its unit?
Are names spelt right? Are the dates, times and job numbers correct?
Have I left out opinions, or marked them clearly?
Have I used a spell checker and a dictionary or manual for trade words?
Is each photo, sketch and table numbered, captioned and in the right place?

ul: If you can, leave the report for a while, then read it again slowly, as if you were the reader.
A spell checker misses real words used wrongly, such as "sheer" for "shear" or "brake" for "break". Read it yourself too.
Ask your supervisor or a co-worker to read it: another person often sees mistakes and unclear parts you miss.
**Sign and date** the report, so it is clear who wrote it and when.
Give it to the **person or office that asked for it**, by the date it is due, and keep a copy.
File paper reports in the right folder by date or job number, in a cabinet that can be locked, and keep them for the time the business sets. They may be needed later if questions come up.
If a filed report turns out to be wrong, do not change or replace it quietly. Issue a **corrected version**, marked as a revision with the date and the reason, and keep the original with it.

blocks.note: Reports often hold private details: customers' names, addresses and phone numbers, prices, and injured people's medical details. Jamaica's data protection law expects personal information to be kept secure and used only for the purpose it was collected for. Share reports only with people who need them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what a technical report is for and think about who will read it.
I can name the common types of report and say when each is used.
I can plan a report: the purpose, the reader, the deadline and the form.
I can gather facts at the time with notes, measurements, photos and sketches, using who, what, when, where, why and how.
I can take a witness's account with open questions, in their own words.
I can tell a fact from an opinion and rewrite a vague statement as a fact.
I can set out a report with a title, introduction, findings, conclusion and numbered recommendations, and say what a summary and an appendix are.
I can write in plain language and explain abbreviations the first time.
I can write measurements with the right units, and write dates and times clearly, including the 24-hour clock.
I can do the simple sums reports need: differences, hours and minutes, percentages and totals.
I can use tables, captioned photos and labelled sketches.
I can write incident, near-miss, inspection, progress and job completion reports and fill in a test record.
I can fill in a form fully, use N/A, and correct a mistake the accepted way.
I can name, save, back up and send a report safely.
I can check a report, sign and date it, hand it to the right person and keep it securely.

terms: A section at the end of a report holding extra material, such as checklists and test sheets
The words under a photo, sketch or table saying what it shows, where and when
The part of a report that sums up what the findings mean
Something that can be seen, measured or checked
The facts, observations and results in a report
A report written after someone is hurt or something is damaged
A report on the condition of an area or equipment after a check
The part of a report that says why it was written and what it covers
A report given to the customer when a job is finished
A question that suggests the answer; not used with witnesses
Not applicable: written in a form box that does not apply
An event that could have caused harm or damage but did not
A question that lets the person answer in their own words
What a person thinks or feels
A file type that looks the same on every device and is hard to change
A report on how far a job has got and what is left
An action the report says should be taken, by whom and by when
A corrected version of a report or drawing, marked with its date and reason
A short paragraph at the start giving the main points
A record of tests carried out, with readings, units, dates and the tester
A form on which workers record the hours they spend on each job
Time written from 00:00 to 23:59, so 2:30 p.m. is 14:30

c1.title: Inspecting the electrical workshop in Lucea
c1.text: Shamar and Alecia, trainees at a training centre in Lucea, Hanover, inspect the Centre's electrical workshop with a checklist on Tuesday 3 November 2026. Their notes include: a dry powder extinguisher by bench 4 with its gauge needle in the red zone; extension lead No. 3 with its outer sheath split for about 40 mm, 150 mm from the plug, showing the coloured inner insulation; a first-aid box with no eyewash and only two plasters; and exit door 2 blocked by a stack of conduit lengths.

c2.title: A falling cylinder in Discovery Bay
c2.text: At a fabrication shop in Discovery Bay, St Ann, a full oxygen cylinder standing unchained beside the cutting bench fell over at about 3:40 p.m. on Thursday 15 October 2026, when a trolley loaded with steel struck it. Nobody was hurt and the valve was not damaged. The cylinder is still lying where it fell; the supervisor, Mr Errol Campbell, has closed off the area and asked trainee Akeem to investigate and write a near-miss report. The trolley driver, Oshane, says the bench blocked his view and that the floor there is often oily.

c3.title: Gates and grilles finished in Brown's Town
c3.text: Kadeem has fitted a pair of steel driveway gates and six window grilles for Mrs Hyacinth Brown in Brown's Town, St Ann, finishing on Friday 30 October 2026. The quotation was for J$385,000. On site, Mrs Brown asked for a padlock bracket that was not in the quotation (J$6,500 extra), and one gate post had to be set 150 mm further back than planned to clear a water pipe. The gates were primed and given two top coats of paint.

c4.title: Wiring a classroom block in Hayes
c4.text: Tishauna, a Level 2 electrical trainee, is helping electrician Mr Neville Gordon wire a new classroom block at a high school in Hayes, Clarendon. Every Friday she writes a progress report for the school's project officer, and she copies the test readings into the test record. This week 4 of the 6 classrooms are wired; the other 2 are waiting for ceiling boards, which were delivered late. Her notebook shows "200" for the insulation resistance of circuit 3, which the tester displayed in megohms.

c5.title: Lost files at a contractor's office in Savanna-la-Mar
c5.text: Garfield runs a small electrical and welding contractor's office in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. His trainee, Jhanielle, types job reports on the office computer and saves them on the desktop with names like "report final 2". Last week the computer failed and three reports were lost. This week a customer pointed out that a report already filed gives the wrong date for his job.

questions.q: Which is the best way to record the extension lead in the findings?
o: One of the extension leads is in a very bad and dangerous state
Lead No. 3 is damaged, and somebody should have reported it before
Lead No. 3: outer sheath split for 40 mm, 150 mm from the plug
Extension lead No. 3 must be thrown away at once and replaced
questions.why: A finding says exactly which item, what is wrong, where and how big, so the reader can act without going to look. Blame and opinions do not belong in the findings, and what to do with the lead belongs in the recommendations.

questions.q: When should Shamar and Alecia tell the supervisor about the blocked exit?
o: In the written report, which is due on Friday
Straight away, before they finish the inspection
At the next monthly safety meeting of the staff
Only if the supervisor asks them about the exits
questions.why: A blocked fire exit could cost lives in an emergency, so it is reported by word of mouth at once. The written report records it afterwards; it never replaces the warning.

questions.q: How should they set out their recommendations?
o: In the order they walked round the workshop, without numbers
In alphabetical order of the items, so they are easy to find
Cheapest first, so the easy jobs get done before the dear ones
Numbered, most urgent first, each saying what, who and by when
questions.why: Numbered recommendations can be followed up one by one. Putting the most dangerous items first, such as the blocked exit and the split lead, makes sure they are dealt with first.

questions.q: The supervisor asks for a short summary at the top of the report. What should it contain?
o: The full checklist, copied out line by line with every tick
How the two trainees felt about the state of the workshop
The main findings and most urgent actions, in a few lines
A list of every tool and machine kept in the workshop
questions.why: A summary gives a busy reader the main points at once. The full checklist belongs in the appendix, and feelings do not belong in a report at all.

questions.q: Before the cylinder is moved, what should Akeem do first, as long as it is safe to leave it?
o: Photograph, measure and sketch the scene as it is
Stand it up and chain it, then write the report from memory
Wait until the end of the day, when the shop is quieter
Ask Oshane to write the report, since he was involved
questions.why: Recording the scene before anything is moved shows exactly where the cylinder, bench and trolley were. Writing from memory later loses details, and the person involved should give a statement, not write the investigation.

questions.q: Which question is most likely to get a full, fair account from Oshane?
o: You were pushing the trolley too fast, weren't you?
Did you see the cylinder standing there before it fell?
Who do you think left the cylinder standing loose there?
Tell me what happened, from when you began to push.
questions.why: An open question lets the witness tell it in their own words. A leading question suggests the answer, a closed question gets only yes or no, and asking who is to blame invites guesses.

questions.q: Which sentence keeps to the facts without blaming anyone?
o: Oshane carelessly drove the trolley into the cylinder at 15:40.
At about 15:40 a loaded trolley struck the unchained cylinder.
The cylinder fell because this shop never cares about safety.
Somebody left the cylinder loose again, as they always do.
questions.why: The fact gives the time, what happened and the condition of the cylinder, all of which can be checked. "Carelessly", "never cares" and "as they always do" are opinions and blame.

questions.q: Which causes should Akeem give in the report?
o: Oshane was not paying attention and should be disciplined
Bad luck: these things happen in any busy fabrication shop
Cylinder unchained, view blocked by the bench, oily floor
The trolley was overloaded and the cylinder was too full
questions.why: The causes are the conditions that let it happen and that can be fixed: chain cylinders, keep the trolley route clear and visible, and clean up oil. Blame and bad luck fix nothing, and a full cylinder is normal.

questions.q: Which details must the completion report explain because they differ from the quotation?
o: The added padlock bracket and the moved post, with reasons
The type and size of electrodes and the welding current used
The names of everyone in the shop who worked on the job
How long each of the six grilles took to make in the shop
questions.why: The customer needs to know what changed from what she agreed to, why, and what it costs. Welding settings and hours are kept on the job card, not in her report.

questions.q: Which care advice is most useful to put in the report?
o: Hose the gates down every day to keep them cool in the sun
Touch up any chips in the paint quickly and oil the hinges
Keep the gates shut at all times so that the hinges last
Paint the gates with any paint left over in the house
questions.why: Bare steel at a chip starts to rust, so touching up paint quickly keeps the gates sound, and oiled hinges work freely. The advice should be practical and in plain words.

questions.q: Why is there space for Mrs Brown to sign the report?
o: To show that she wrote the report herself
To confirm she accepts the work as complete
To give the shop permission to visit again
To make the report her receipt for the tax office
questions.why: The customer's signature records that she agrees the work described is finished. If questions come up later, the signed report shows what was done and accepted.

questions.q: What total price should the report show for the job?
questions.why: J$385,000 + J$6,500 = J$391,500. The report should show the quoted price, the extra and the new total, so the customer can see how it was worked out.

questions.q: What should the progress report say about the two unfinished classrooms?
o: Why they are waiting, and when work should start again
Nothing, since only finished work goes in a progress report
That the delay is the supplier's fault and not the team's
That they will be finished on time, to keep the officer happy
questions.why: A progress report gives what is done, what is left, the reasons for any delay and what happens next. Blame and promises the facts do not support make the report less useful.

questions.q: How should the reading for circuit 3 be written in the test record?
o: 200 MΩ against circuit 3, with the test date
200, since everyone knows the unit for this test
200 Ω, since resistance is always given in ohms
Good, since a number means little to the reader
questions.why: A reading needs its unit, written exactly as the instrument showed it (megohms here), against the right circuit and with the date. Without the unit, 200 could mean anything.

questions.q: What percentage of the classrooms should Tishauna report as wired?
o: About 33%
About 40%
About 4%
About 67%
questions.why: 4 ÷ 6 × 100 ≈ 67%. It is clearest to give both: "4 of the 6 classrooms (about 67%) are wired."

questions.q: Which file name and place are best for a finished report?
o: report final final 2.docx, on the desktop where it is easy to find
2026-11-03_Job1142_completion.pdf, in the agreed jobs folder
new report Garfield.docx, in the downloads folder for now
a photo of the printed report, on Jhanielle's own phone
questions.why: A name with the date, job number and type of report can be found and sorted easily, and the agreed folder is the one that is backed up. Files on the desktop or a personal phone are easily lost or seen by the wrong people.

questions.q: How should the office stop reports being lost again?
o: Print every report and delete the files to free up space
Keep all the reports on one USB stick in the cash drawer
Back up the jobs folder often to a second, separate place
Email the reports to Jhanielle's personal address as well
questions.why: A regular backup to a second place means one failure cannot destroy the only copy. A single USB stick can be lost too, and personal email puts customers' details where they should not be.

questions.q: What should Jhanielle do about the filed report that gives the wrong date?
o: Change the date in the saved file and save over the old one
Leave it as it is, since the job is finished and paid for
Delete the old file and write a new report from memory
Issue a corrected revision, dated, and keep the original
questions.why: A corrected version marked as a revision, with the date and reason, keeps an honest record of what changed. Saving over the original hides the change, which matters if the report is ever used as evidence.

questions.q: Which sentence writes the measurement correctly?
o: The gap measured 2.5mms.
The gap measured 2,5 MM.
The gap measured 2.5 mm.
The gap measured .25 cm's.
questions.why: Write the number with a decimal point, a space, then the unit symbol in the right letters, with no s and no apostrophe: 2.5 mm.

questions.q: A report will be read by a supplier in the United States. How should the date 7 November 2026 be written?
o: 07/11/2026, the Jamaican way
11/07/2026, the American way
2026/11/07, the computer way
7 November 2026
questions.why: Jamaicans read 07/11/2026 as 7 November, but an American reader takes it as 11 July. Writing the month in words cannot be misread by anyone.
